strengths: The paper introduces an important and clearly motivated NLP/code-reasoning task: verifying whether scientific code faithfully implements its accompanying paper. The distinction among differences, paper omissions, and code omissions is useful.
The 81 real discrepancies are grounded in GitHub issues and reproducibility reports, while versioned papers and repository commits help preserve the evidence underlying each example.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 21 proprietary and open-weight models. Exact model variants, prompts, decoding settings, preprocessing, and context handling are documented, and the code-only ablation helps establish that the paper contributes information beyond the repository alone.

The authors recognize incomplete ground truth and perform a valuable follow-up audit of unmatched predictions on 12 NLP papers. This analysis shows that models find additional valid discrepancies and provides initial precision estimates rather than reporting reference recall uncritically.
The paper is clearly organized, relevant to ACL, and provides informative analyses by discrepancy source, type, context length, publication year, and programming language.
weaknesses: The synthetic subset constitutes 530 of the 611 examples but lacks adequate independent validation. GPT-5 generates the modifications and labels, and the reported checks establish only that edits are small and apply cleanly—not that they execute, preserve surrounding functionality, represent realistic scientific mismatches, or satisfy the paper's significance definition. Human expert validation of a statistically meaningful sample is needed.

The claim that synthetic data are a reliable proxy for real discrepancies is not supported by the reported correlation alone. A high correlation of model-level recalls across 21 models can arise from general model capability and does not establish similarity in error distributions, construct validity, or absolute difficulty. Moreover, GPT-5 both generates the synthetic data and ranks first on it, creating generator-specific artifact and self-preference concerns.

Real-data ground-truth construction is insufficiently documented for a benchmark. Candidate filtering is described as manual, but the number and expertise of annotators, independent annotation, adjudication, and agreement are not reported. Final verification and standardized descriptions rely on GPT-5. Recall of the Qwen prefilter is also not measured, so the collection may systematically omit harder discrepancy types.

The primary evaluation uses an incomplete reference set and an LLM judge from the GPT-OSS family. Judge validation is based on embedding-selected top-three candidates for only 20 discrepancies, rather than a representative sample of all evaluated pairs. This may inflate agreement and is particularly concerning when interpreting GPT-OSS results. The later 12-paper audit is useful but selectively restricted to NLP and its pooled set is not demonstrably comprehensive.

Models with different context windows receive different truncated inputs: entire code files are removed from the end until each model's prompt fits. Consequently, some models may not receive the evidence needed for a discrepancy, confounding comparisons among models as well as the context-length analysis. Repository ordering and the frequency and impact of truncation are not reported.

Several conclusions are overstated. Lower performance on 2025 papers does not demonstrate that older papers and code were memorized; publication year is confounded with source, repository size, domain, and discrepancy type. Likewise, the code-only experiment supports the utility of paper input but does not establish multimodality, since both inputs are textual and repositories may reproduce paper content in README files.

Results on only 81 real discrepancies—sometimes divided into very small subgroups—are reported without confidence intervals or significance tests. This limits confidence in model rankings and analyses by type, year, and source.

Reproducibility is only partial because core construction depends on proprietary GPT-5 and Mistral OCR services. The paper states that the dataset is public, but the manuscript does not provide a clear archival link or enough release details to verify that all versioned inputs, generated patches, annotations, and evaluation code will be available. These unresolved validity issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although they appear addressable in a substantial revision.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored NLP/code-understanding problem: checking whether scientific code faithfully implements the accompanying paper. The task is relevant to reproducibility, automated reviewing, and scientific agents.

SCICOQA combines naturally occurring discrepancies from GitHub issues and reproducibility reports with controlled synthetic modifications. Versioning papers and repositories to the time at which discrepancies were reported is particularly thoughtful.
The paper provides clear discrepancy definitions and taxonomies, full prompts, model identifiers, context limits, and preprocessing details. The presentation and examples are generally clear.

The evaluation covers 21 contemporary models and includes useful analyses by discrepancy type, source, context length, publication year, programming language, and paper-plus-code versus code-only input. The small manual study of unmatched predictions usefully exposes incompleteness in the initial labels.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claim is not adequately supported. The reported 45.7% is recall on 81 source-selected, partially model-filtered reference discrepancies—not the proportion of all real-world paper-code discrepancies detected. The authors' own pooled annotation of only 12 selected NLP papers substantially changes recall and discovers many additional discrepancies, demonstrating that the original ground truth is incomplete. Claims about assuring faithfulness or detecting real-world discrepancies should be narrowed accordingly.

Input construction can make the target evidence unavailable. For models whose context window is exceeded, entire code files are removed from the end without checking whether the file containing the reference discrepancy remains. Figures are also removed from papers. Because context limits vary greatly across models, this confounds model comparisons, long-context analyses, and domain results; some recorded failures may be impossible instances rather than reasoning failures. The paper should report target-evidence retention and use a controlled retrieval or evidence-preserving protocol.

Ground-truth quality control is insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not report the number or expertise of human annotators, independent annotation, agreement, adjudication, or a human audit of the final 81 examples. Manual filtering is followed by GPT-5 verification and standardized rewriting, while GPT-5 also generates all synthetic discrepancies and is a principal evaluated system. This creates model-specific selection and stylistic leakage risks.

The synthetic-data validation is weak. Minimal edit size and code-level Jaccard similarity do not establish that injected discrepancies are realistic, scientifically meaningful, executable, or comparable in difficulty to naturally occurring discrepancies. The correlation of aggregate real and synthetic recall across 21 models can be explained by general model capability and does not establish that synthetic instances are an unbiased proxy. No expert validation or execution-based check of a representative synthetic sample is reported.

Evaluation relies on a GPT-OSS-20B judge whose validation covers only 20 reference discrepancies and embedding-selected top-three candidate predictions. This sampling does not clearly test the judge over the full distribution of outputs and models. Precision is otherwise estimated post hoc on just 12 deliberately selected NLP papers, using outputs from three models to expand the gold set, so the broad statement that leading systems are precise remains tentative.

Results lack uncertainty estimates over benchmark sampling and generation. Predictions appear to come from one high-temperature run, despite temperature 1.0, while only judge variability is measured. Multiple discrepancies from the same paper are also treated as separate observations without accounting for clustering. Several causal interpretations—especially the claim that lower 2025 performance demonstrates pretraining contamination—are unsupported by controls or significance analyses.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the PDF contains no accessible code or data link, despite stating that the dataset is publicly released, so the examples, repository snapshots, splits, scripts, and reported scores cannot be independently checked from the submission. Overall, the task and dataset direction are promising, but the evidence-availability confound, incomplete and circularly validated labels, limited judge validation, and absent accessible artifacts prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation. These issues seem addressable with substantial re-evaluation rather than fundamental reconstruction, motivating a resubmit-next-cycle score.

strengths: SCICOQA addresses an important and underexplored NLP/code-understanding problem: determining whether scientific code faithfully implements its accompanying paper. The task is well motivated and highly relevant to reproducibility, automated reviewing, and scientific agents.

The dataset combines 81 real discrepancies from GitHub issues and reproducibility reports with 530 controlled synthetic discrepancies, and it includes useful taxonomies covering discrepancy type and affected research component.

The empirical study is unusually broad, evaluating 21 proprietary and open-weight models. The paper also provides informative analyses by discrepancy origin, type, context length, publication year, programming language, and paper-plus-code versus code-only input.

The authors make meaningful efforts to validate the evaluation: they manually label 1,039 candidate-reference pairs, assess unmatched predictions for three leading models, and construct a more comprehensive pooled ground truth for 12 NLP papers. These checks support the main qualitative conclusion that current systems have limited recall despite sometimes high precision.

The paper is clearly written, well organized, visually polished, and commendably explicit about prompts, repository versioning, OCR, file filtering, decoding settings, and model versions. Overall, this is a promising contribution near the main-conference threshold. weaknesses: The strongest validity claim about the synthetic subset is insufficiently supported. A Pearson correlation of 0.94 across 21 related model variants shows similar model ranking, but does not establish that synthetic discrepancies resemble real discrepancies or form a reliable proxy for real-world performance. The subsets differ substantially in difficulty and type distribution, while the reported edit size and Jaccard similarity do not validate semantic realism. Human assessment of a representative synthetic sample is needed.

Dataset construction depends heavily on GPT-5: it extracts and finally verifies real discrepancies, generates standardized references, creates all synthetic discrepancies, and is then itself benchmarked. Manual filtering helps, but the paper does not report annotator counts, independent final human verification, agreement, or detailed adjudication. This leaves risks of model-specific artifacts and circular preference, especially in the synthetic results.

The automatic judge validation is limited to 20 real discrepancies and candidates preselected using embedding similarity. It is unclear how well the reported 87.5 F1 transfers across domains, synthetic cases, discrepancy types, and models with different writing styles. The acknowledged self-preference of the GPT-OSS judge further complicates comparisons involving GPT-OSS outputs.

For inputs exceeding a model's context window, entire code files are removed from the end of the prompt. The paper does not report whether the file containing each reference discrepancy remains visible. Consequently, some measured failures—especially for shorter-context models—may arise because the necessary evidence was removed, confounding model capability with context-window size and unspecified file ordering.

Several causal or general claims are overstated. Poorer results on 2025 papers do not by themselves demonstrate benefit from pretraining contamination because publication year is confounded with repository length, domain, and discrepancy composition. Likewise, precision is established only for three models on 12 selected NLP papers, so the broader statement that the best models are precise should be qualified.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the reviewed manuscript: the code and data fields are blank, despite a stated public release, and no executable evaluation pipeline is linked. Reliance on proprietary GPT-5 and MistralOCR also limits exact reconstruction. The stochastic model generations appear to use one run without uncertainty estimates, while only the judge is repeated.

The prediction prompt is not fully aligned with the benchmark taxonomy: it broadly says that missing paper information and missing implementations do not count, while paper omissions and code omissions are two central target types. The intended distinction from trivial missing details or wholly unavailable implementations should be made explicit to avoid suppressing valid predictions. There is also a mislabeled count order in Table 5's type row and an unexplained apparent discrepancy between 67 real plus 204 synthetic source papers and the reported total of 266 papers.
